phases: The Words of the Unwritten Rule

listenings.text: Every workplace runs on two sets of rules. The first one is written down, and you can read it on your first morning. The second one is not written anywhere, and it is the one that actually decides how people see you. Nobody teaches it, because the people who know it have stopped noticing that it exists. So you learn it the only way there is, which is by breaking it and watching what happens to the room. A small silence, a slightly too quick change of subject, an email that gets answered in one line when the others get five. None of that is punishment. It is information, and it is the only information available. The mistake is to read it as a judgement about you. It is a map, and the sooner you start drawing it, the sooner the place stops feeling foreign.

Two things caught me out in my first year working with a team in the United Kingdom, and neither of them was the language. The first was the evening. I would answer an email at nine at night and feel efficient, and it slowly became clear that nobody expected it and one or two people found it uncomfortable. Not wrong, exactly. Just not done. The second one was harder. In a meeting I would say what I thought, plainly, the way I would at home, and I could see it land as much stronger than I meant it. The same sentence carried more weight in that room than in mine. I did not change what I thought and I did not start hiding my opinion. I changed the first four words of the sentence, and that turned out to be enough.
